idiom_name: null / default(T) / null! placeholder, Moq Mock.Of<T>() as the toolkit route
implementation_notes: Reference-typed slots take null, which is the placeholder of choice, and generic slots take default(T) (null for reference types, an all-zero value for value types). Once nullable reference types are enabled the compiler demands an explicit escape: the null-forgiving operator (null!) or a nullable local, and the escape should stay local to the call site. Where an interface must be a non-null instance, a test-local empty class is the honest placeholder, while Moq's LINQ to Mocks form Mock.Of<T>() fabricates one in a single expression - but an unconfigured mock is loose, answers every member with a default and therefore stops being a dummy as soon as the path reads the parameter. Discards (a parameter named _) document the callee side, where C# raises no warning for unused parameters.
pitfalls: null! silences nullable analysis at exactly the point where the assumption lives: a placeholder threaded through an NRT-enabled API also hides real null-safety defects in the same expression, so keep the escape on the argument, not on the field.
An unconfigured Moq mock is loose by default and returns defaults for every member, so if the path starts reading the placeholder the test may keep passing with fabricated data instead of failing.

default(T) for a struct parameter is the all-zero value and can violate the type's invariants (a null string inside a record, a zero enumeration); a placeholder struct that the callee validates will fail in a way that looks unrelated to the test's intent.
